title: David Law calls for 'change' to DP World Tour schedule over mental health concern
article_text:
David Law believes the latter part of the regular DP World Tour season “needs to change” after feeling that players battling it out for various reasons are being left exhausted.

The Aberdonian just held on to his Category 10 card after playing 11 weeks in a row, a marathon stretch that started in Denmark in mid-August and ended in Korea last week.

American Sean Crocker, who claimed the final Category 10 card after the Genesis Championship on Sunday, did likewise and spoke about how he’d been away from home for 12 weeks in total.

“The one thing I feel is that the schedule needs to change a little bit on the tour,” Law, delighted to have joined Calum Hill, Grant Forrest, Ewen Ferguson, Bob MacIntyre, Scott Jamieson and Connor Syme in securing his full status for the 2027 campaign, told The Scotsman.

“I think having 11 weeks in a row at the end of the year when you have guys fighting for jobs, guys fighting for PGA Tour cards and guys fighting to get into the Play-Offs is a bit much.

“I think finishing the season off after we’ve been in Europe for so long to go out to India and Korea with the time difference and have those as the last two counting events is pretty poor, to be honest.

“I just feel it’s not fair on guys in the situation I found myself in to be expected to play that much, especially with the uncertainty of those entry lists, which were staying so high for so long.”

While Law is looking forward to spending four weeks at home before starting the new campaign in Australia at the end of next month, players who fell short in the card battle are now set to be involved in this week’s Second Stage of the DP World Tour Qualifying School in Spain.

“I’m absolutely done in, both physically and mentally,” declared Law, who played in 30 events during the year, with only a handful of players having teed up more than the 35-year-old. “If I didn’t keep my card and had to go to the Q School next week, I don’t think I’d have any chance of competing, to be honest, and I know there are 20-30 guys who are in the exact same boat as me.

“Mental health and well being and stuff like that is spoken about a lot these days and I don’t think that last closing stretch is fair on the players and I think something needs to change.”

Next year’s schedule has already been announced - the final regular event will still be in the Far East, though a trip to Hong Kong rather than Korea - but changes could be afoot in 2028.

“Next season, I have a huge motivation to make sure I am not in the same position again and, hopefully, this time next year I am gearing up for going to the Middle East rather than trying to keep my card,” said Law, the 2019 ISPS HANDA Vic Open winner.

This season, Law played in two Rolex Series events - the Hero Dubai Desert Classic and the BMW PGA Championship - but missed out on the Genesis Scottish Open. However, he added: "Finishing in the top 100 makes a big difference in terms of scheduling and playing in the bigger events next year."

title: LIV Golf’s collapse leaves the DP World Tour facing a promise it can’t afford to keep
article_text:
In the moment his week went without a headline. Charles Howell III finished his 54-hole trek around the Old Course, Carnoustie and Kingsbarns one shot on the wrong side of the cut line at the Alfred Dunhill Links earlier this month. No offense to Howell, who has put together a good career, but at 47 his results stopped being notable long ago. Except that performance is newsworthy now, because it appears those rounds were an audition. And that he’s being considered at all has irritated DP World Tour regulars, hinting at a larger mess. LIV Golf has imploded, and the European circuit must sift through the debris without cutting itself.

Interestingly, it is rubble the DP World Tour helped cause. While LIV has had too many self-inflicted wounds to list, what hindsight might consider the nascent league's knockout blow came from the DP World Tour CEO Guy Kinnings when he announced his league would no longer grant conditional releases to LIV players next year. “Players need to make a choice,” Kinnings told the BBC. “We have rules and regulations which are there to protect our tour and which our members must all abide by. Players who are not willing to comply with our rules and regulations should not be seeking to join our tour.” LIV golfers could no longer double-dip, and European players like Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton would lose Ryder Cup eligibility if they did not side with the DP World Tour. In turn, the bulk of LIV’s already-thin roster of formidable players have since signaled their intention to leave.

The old-world circuit’s move was partially defensive. Despite LIV Golf CEO Scott O’Neil saying his league wanted to “complete, not compete” the professional golf landscape, LIV had scrambled to poach DP World Tour events and sponsors for its next iteration, and that was after raiding the DP World Tour’s roster since 2022. Enough was enough. There was an upside to this calculus, too. The PGA Tour has no appetite to lift its LIV suspensions, which leaves those players desperately searching for a landing spot. A half-dozen of them would bolster DPWT fields depleted in the last few seasons by the LIV exodus along with the tour’s best players graduating to the PGA Tour.

Frankly, the DP World Tour needs the help. The tour’s 2025 numbers show a pre-tax profit of a little more than $4 million. Beneath it runs an operating loss of $85 million, sheltered by the PGA Tour helping with roughly $77 million in cash. Worse, the DP World Tour’s media-rights deal plummeted. The PGA Tour owns 30 percent of European Tour Productions, with a clause at the end of 2027 that lets the PGA Tour hand those shares back or allow the DP World Tour to buy them.

Meaning, the DP World Tour is struggling to pay its bills, and the entity helping them cover its costs could be out of the arrangement in 14 months.

Stars sell broadcast rights and sponsorships, and the DP World Tour has few of them to spare. Rahm, Hatton and Bryson DeChambeau in a field during the lean summer months are worth real money to a tour that can no longer assume someone else will cover the shortfall. The strategic alliance between the PGA Tour and DP World Tour is strong, and Kinnings (below) and new PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp have a good rapport. But does a post-LIV world challenge that relationship?

LIV’s Lee Westwood, who since settling his fines with the DP World Tour has appointed himself its civics teacher, wrote on social media that anyone who believes the PGA Tour is a DP World Tour partner instead of a rival is “either blind or fools.” Westy has been a bad-faith actor on many of golf’s issues during the schism he helped instigate. On this front, though, he has a point. Partners don’t usually come with exit clauses. If the PGA Tour can walk away from its stake next year, the DP World Tour has every reason to build a product that can stand without it, and the quickest way to do that runs through the players the PGA Tour still won’t let back in.

However, the bill for all this lands on those who stayed. Since a number of LIV players don’t have DP World Tour status, they will need sponsor’s invitations, and word among members and agents is the tour may offer 10-plus exemptions to certain LIV players. Understandably, this has not gone over well with those already on the DP World Tour, who risk getting squeezed out should LIV players get those invites. Joost Luiten said that LIV players “didn’t give a s***” about the DP World Tour when they left, and that they should have to go to Q-School. Ewen Ferguson found it comical that those who spent golf’s civil war torching the establishment act like they are coming home. Richard Mansell agreed, although he said that some should be allowed back and others should not. Basically, the rank-and-file want to know why is their tour turning from the men who stayed loyal to welcome back those who didn’t mind burning it down?

"As someone who has gone through the wringer this game provides (mostly due to my own shortcomings of course) in recent years, and who has gone back to Q School and had two immensely divergent experiences, betrayal feels like the right word," wrote DP World Tour player Eddie Pepperell in a thoughtful piece over the weekend. "And unfortunately when one feels that way inevitably what follows is a loss of respect, and what tends to fill the void left behind is resentment and contempt."

title: DP World Tour pros hit back at plans for LIV golfers
article_text:
Get the latest news, reviews, analysis and opinion, plus unmissable deals and exclusive offers. Please check the box of every email you wish to receive.

A group of DP World Tour pros have raised issue with the circuit’s proposals to offer spots in 2027 to LIV golfers.

As doubt continues to grow over the future of the breakaway circuit, the DP World Tour is looking at ways to incorporate both non-members and returning members in 2027, if they cut ties with the LIV setup.

From 2027, players will no longer be able to play across both the DP World Tour and LIV, which has led to the likes of Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton and Tom McKibbin quitting the latter amid its 2.0 plans.

In the wake of this, bunkered.co.uk understands that the DP World Tour has received a high volume of interest from LIV competitors, especially from those who currently have no status.

A well-placed DP World Tour source also informed bunkered.co.uk that those in charge at Wentworth HQ are in ‘advanced conversations’ with players showing interest in tournament invites.

It is understood that these players are in line to receive guaranteed invites to a specific number of DP World Tour tournaments, excluding the elevated Rolex Series events.

Existing members meanwhile are able to return to their specific category, so long as they have ended their relationship with the LIV setup.

The proposals to integrate both members and non-members has seemingly split opinion among those who opted to remain with the DP World Tour.

Taking to X, Ewen Ferguson wrote: “I have to say, some of the LIV players coming back to play DP [World Tour] is actually cool as some really good players.

“But hilarious how some of them slammed the tour for so long, not one good thing to say about it, now it’s the best thing since sliced bread and feels like coming home.”

This spurred a response from 25-time winner, and LIV golfer, Lee Westwood, who resigned his DP World Tour membership back in 2023 on the back of his Saudi switch.

“It’s an interesting position the @DPWorldTour finds itself in,” said Westwood. “Caught between needing ‘names’ at those times of year when they don’t get strong fields (Jan-June).

“Giving invites to people who have shown no interest in the tour other than now when they’ve nowhere else to play. And keeping the members happy that support the tour at the smaller events and the lads that have gone through all the qualifying stages.

“Anyone with an exemption should be free to come back because as we know the DPWT endorses members going to another rival tour and already have 10 cards for it but if people don’t have an exemption they should have to go through the school like everyone else.

“Anyone that thinks the PGA Tour aren’t rivals and are partners are either blind or fools.”

As well as Westwood, Ferguson’s post caught the attention of fellow member, Richard Mansell, who backed up the Scot’s comments. “Spot on my mate,” Mansell tweeted.

“I haven’t been around the tour a lot this year and when I have since coming back from injury my golf hasn’t been where I want it so I don’t want to say too much. However, things are going to look different in 2027. Some should be allowed back and some shouldn’t…”

Three-time DP World Tour winner, Jorge Campillo added: “Are we giving cards away for free. How are they getting one?” Eddie Pepperell has been as outspoken as any pro against the LIV setup in recent years.

He too had his say last weekend in a lengthy article via The Chipping Forecast’s substack.

Pepperrell wrote: “To give playing opportunities to LIV golfers, those very people who proudly represented an entity that put your own business in jeopardy, ahead of folks like myself, and others it should be said, who go to Q School and incarnate the very principles that make golf what it is, also represents a betrayal.”

His point was backed by the DP World Tour’s No. 2 player for 2025, Marco Penge, who replied on X: “Well said, its pretty simple. I think the reason for leaving the DP World Tour to go to LIV kinda speaks for itself.”

Similar points were raised by the likes of Matt Wallace, James Morrison and Danny Willett to bunkered.co.uk earlier this summer at the Husqvarna British Masters.

While those who have kept the DP World Tour close by during their time with LIV look to be under little fire, the issue seemingly lies with those who walked away, or have paid no previous attention to the European circuit.

The concern over playing opportunities being swarmed by LIV golfers, though, was eased by Pepperell, who lost his card on Sunday after finishing 101st in the Race to Dubai rankings.

The Englishman revealed that due to recent restrictions on the number of full cards via the rankings, the HotelPlanner Tour and Q School, around 25-30 spots will be freed up to those lower down the food chain.

Effectively, the number of cards has reduced, but the number of tournament spots have not. The only ‘wrinkle’ – as Pepperell put it – is just how many of those spots will be handed to those jumping the LIV ship.

title: Newcastle United signs Taittinger champagne partnership
article_text:
Newcastle United has agreed a multi-year partnership with French champagne house Taittinger, expanding the club’s premium hospitality offering at St James’ Park following a £10m investment in its facilities.

Under the agreement, Taittinger becomes Newcastle’s champagne partner, with its products served across premium hospitality suites, executive boxes and selected club events.

The partnership will see Taittinger’s Brut Réserve and Prestige Rosé available to hospitality guests, alongside Domaine Evremond Classic Cuvée, the champagne producer’s English sparkling wine.

The deal follows Newcastle’s £10m hospitality redevelopment programme, completed over the summer, which has focused on upgrading premium areas and improving the matchday experience for corporate guests and supporters.

Taittinger has an established history of partnerships with major sporting and cultural events, including previous involvement with the FIFA World Cup.

For Newcastle, the agreement adds another international brand to its commercial portfolio while supporting the club’s investment in premium matchday experiences and hospitality revenues.

Dave O’Connor, Chief Revenue Officer at Newcastle United, said, “The Taittinger family has a long and proud history of partnering with some of the world’s most prestigious sporting events. We are delighted that they have chosen to continue their football journey with Newcastle United.“

“Their decision to partner with us is a reflection of the ambition we have as a club and our commitment to consistently raising the bar. We look forward to working together as we set new benchmarks for luxury matchday hospitality at St. James’ Park and create exceptional experiences for our fans.“

Mills Easby, UK Director at Taittinger, said, “The Taittinger family are delighted to be partnering with Newcastle United, a club that is not only an icon of English Football but one that sits so solidly as the beating heart of the North East. It is an immensely exciting time to be getting involved at St. James’ Park and we look forward to sharing some truly memorable moments with you all.“

title: Report: China’s CCTV drops LaLiga coverage over Mbappe comments
article_text:
CCTV, the Chinese state broadcaster, has suspended its coverage of Spanish soccer's top-tier LaLiga, due to social media videos involving Kylian Mbappe, the Real Madrid and France superstar.

Various Chinese media outlets have reported that CCTV has taken this decision following a comment made by Mbappe in a recent interview, in which he referred to former Chinese national leader and icon Mao Zedong as a "dictator."

Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms.

Mbappe had been questioned about his favorite meme, and responded by mentioning an internet picture in which his face is placed onto a portrait of Mao.

Specifically, Mbappe – who has now also been dropped by several prominent Chinese brands – said: "The [meme] that made me laugh the most is the one where they put my face on a Chinese dictator."

CCTV, it has been reported, will also not be broadcasting any fixtures involving Mbappe – for example, in the pan-European UEFA Champions League – for the moment.

Satire involving depictions of former Chinese Communist Party leaders and figures can form a punishable offence in China, due to laws which prohibit "defamation of heroes and martyrs."

Mao died in 1976, and any jokes about the former leader are seen in China as a social taboo.

CCTV (owned by China Media Group) had snapped up LaLiga rights for the ongoing 2026-27 season in mid-August, with the tie-up covering both free-to-air and pay-TV rights.

The league is also covered in China by major digital streaming platform Migu, through a four-campaign tie-up.

It has also had a physical office in Shanghai since 2014 – and Mbappe is seen as its most recognizable face.

Meanwhile, two major Chinese brands have ended their association with Mbappe over the incident: drinks heavyweight Dongpeng and dairy conglomerate Mengniu.

Mengniu, in a statement, said: "With immediate effect our company is terminating all cooperation with Kylian Mbappe. Mengniu firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people."

Dongpeng stated that it has the same approach towards "any behaviour that offends national sentiments."

In terms of recent criticism of Spanish soccer by China over similar incidents, last month, Chinese state media said that Real Madrid's messages of support to Tibet and Nepal following mass flooding in those regions featured "incorrect" wording.

In April, meanwhile, fellow LaLiga giants Barcelona apologised after a flag of disputed island Taiwan appeared on an online site linked to its international academy.

title: Ineos puts FC Lausanne-Sport on market as sports downsizing continues
Charlotte FC, Ally agree to extend front-of-kit sponsorship into 2030s
article_text:
Ally Financial will remain Charlotte FC’s front-of-kit sponsor well into the next decade after extending a partnership that dates to the MLS club’s inaugural season in 2022. The sides reached the agreement with multiple seasons remaining on the current deal, in part to account for MLS’s move to a summer-to-spring calendar next year.

Financial terms and the precise duration of the extension were not disclosed. The Charlotte Business Journal reported the bank is paying an average of $8M per year under the current deal. MLS front-of-kit sponsorships are typically valued in the mid-seven-figure range annually, with SponsorUnited estimating the average this season at $5.1M.

In addition to being Charlotte FC’s most lucrative sponsorship, Ally Chief Marketing and PR Officer Andrea Brimmer said it is one of the bank’s largest investments when considering “sponsorship fees, as well as the activation.”

“One thing about Ally that makes this so rewarding is how heavily involved they are in activation and engagement,” said Tepper Sports & Entertainment CRO Eric Sudol. “Andrea and her team understand what the definition of success is. We know the KPIs and the bogeys that we’re up against. So, if you’re hitting those along the way, then by all means you continue.”

The sponsorship package will largely remain the same, with the front-of-kit placement serving as the core asset. Ally will continue to sponsor the Pitches for Progress community initiative through which the partners have opened seven mini-pitches in at-risk communities. The brand’s logo is also displayed in the center circle during team entrances before each match.

“We had over 500 Ally employees that have had an opportunity to volunteer through the partnership, which we really like,” Brimmer said. “And then, just the ability to have everything from the media to the in-stadium signage to the rights to use the logo and the marks, especially with a really hot soccer calendar. So, all of those things persist. It’s been a pretty robust deal. We’re really doubling down on the things that we’ve done and just being creative with them as we go forward.”

Brimmer said the Charlotte FC deal has driven positive business results, including a 22% jump in Ally’s brand awareness among MLS fans. The Detroit-based digital financial services firm maintains its largest employment hub in Uptown Charlotte, and Brimmer said the MLS club partnership has helped attract and retain talent. The bank also soft-launched its new customer loyalty program, Loyally, with Charlotte FC fans this season before rolling it out nationwide.

One unusual wrinkle of the relationship between Charlotte FC and Ally is that the team plays in a stadium named for Bank of America, a competitor to Ally in financial services. Tepper Sports & Entertainment, which owns both Charlotte FC and the Carolina Panthers, signed a long-term extension of its naming-rights agreement with Bank of America earlier this year.

That agreement limits the stadium-specific assets TS&E can offer Ally, including naming rights to premium spaces, but the two financial institutions have worked to ensure their sponsorship assets do not conflict.

“It is unique, but we’ve had a lot of direct conversation with the leadership at Bank of America and just worked through it so that we both can protect our assets and protect our investment, but do it in a way that doesn’t compete with one another,” Brimmer said.

The Ally extension comes as Bank of America Stadium and its surrounding campus undergo a $1.3B transformation. Sudol said TS&E is in the market with sponsorship inventory tied to new premium spaces and expects the renovated facility to have at least eight “cornerstone” partners (in addition to Bank of America) when it opens by the start of the 2030 MLS and NFL seasons.

title: Badminton: Aaron-Wooi Yik won't let injury derail their late surge to earn World Tour Finals ticket
article_text:
PETALING JAYA: A minor injury will not derail men’s doubles pair Aaron Chia-Soh Wooi Yik’s late surge to secure qualification for the season-ending World Tour Finals.

The duo were forced to retire from their French Open quarter-final match against eventual champions Man Wei Chong-Tee Kai Wun last Friday due to Wooi Yik suffering a right heel injury.

That withdrawal, combined with skipping the Hylo Open in Germany, leaves the pair fifth in the race for the coveted eight spots for the Finals in Hangzhou from Dec 9-13.

Despite the setback, Aaron confirmed that qualifying remains the top priority for the world No. 4 pair as they face a packed November schedule, beginning with the Korean Open (Nov 3-8), followed by the Kumamoto Masters (Nov 10-15), and concluding with the Hong Kong Open (Nov 17-22).

“We have to go all out because there are still three tournaments left,” said Aaron upon arriving at Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) yesterday.

“There are points to be earned, so we will compete and see how things turn out.”

Aaron, 29, also confirmed that his partner Wooi Yik, 28, is recovering well, describing the situation as “not serious”.

“Everything is good in terms of his condition.

“He is still recovering, but we will definitely be going to Korea, Japan and Hong Kong.”

Recently reunited after a brief split, Aaron-Wooi Yik proved they remain a formidable force by reaching the Denmark Open final just a week before their quarter-final withdrawal in Paris.

“We’ve been playing together for many years, so it (the split) didn’t really affect us that much,” he said.

However, he preferred to temper expectations of a deep run at the Finals.

“Let's qualify first, then we can think about the knockout stages.''

Aaron-Wooi Yik have never advanced past the group stage in their four previous attempts in 2019, 2020, 2023 and 2025.

Meanwhile, world No. 5 Goh Sze Fei-Nur Izzuddin Rumsani, the 2024 Finals silver medalists, have already secured their qualification. Only two entries per nation are allowed in the Finals.

title: PV Sindhu climbs three spots to reach World no 8 in BWF World Rankings
article_text:
The star Indian shuttler PV Sindhu returns to the world top 8 after her runner-up finish at the recently concluded French Open, leaping up three spots in BWF rankings on Tuesday.

Sindhu had a tremendous week, looking much more precise on her returns and showing glimpses of her best form throughout the tournament.

She reached her first-ever French Open final in Paris, beating Japan’s Hina Akechi in a three-game semi-final. In the final, she took the first game off World No. 1 An Se Young of South Korea but ultimately lost 21-16, 11-21, 12-21.

This helped her return to the world top 8 for the first time in three months since her Japan Open triumph in July 2026 and further boosted her chances of qualifying for the World Tour Finals.

Meanwhile, Asmita Chaliha, who defeated world No. 3 Akane Yamaguchi en route to the quarter-finals of the French Open, climbed six places to world rank No. 30.

She has now become the fourth Indian women’s singles player inside the top 30, following Unnati Hooda (21st) and Tanvi Sharma (22nd), who dropped three places and one place, respectively, in the latest rankings.

title: Jannik Sinner set for a potential return after knee injury as Six Kings Slam rescheduled to December
article_text:
World No. 1 Jannik Sinner is set to return to action at the Six Kings Slam in Saudi Arabia in December after the lucrative exhibition tournament was postponed from its original October dates amid security concerns in the region, Reuters reported on Monday.

The Italian had announced earlier this month that he would not compete again in 2026 as he continued his recovery from a knee injury that has kept him out of action since his Wimbledon triumph in July. However, the revised schedule for the Six Kings Slam could see the two-time defending champion make a comeback before the end of the year.

The exhibition event, which was originally scheduled to take place in Riyadh from October 21 to 24, has been rescheduled for December 27 to 30.

Sinner's potential return at the Six Kings Slam comes after a period on the sidelines following his Wimbledon victory in July. The 25-year-old had indicated that he would skip the European indoor hard-court season and the ATP Finals in Turin, where he has won the title in each of the last two editions.

His participation in the rescheduled exhibition would therefore mark a significant development in his recovery, although it remains separate from his official ATP Tour commitments.

Sinner has dominated the Six Kings Slam since its introduction, beating Spanish rival Carlos Alcaraz in both finals. The Italian earned $6 million for each victory, underlining the extraordinary financial rewards on offer at the non-ATP event.

, Alexander Zverev, Taylor Fritz and Alex de Minaur. The presence of several of the sport's leading names is expected to make the December event one of the most closely watched exhibitions on the tennis calendar. With Sinner and Alcaraz having contested the previous two finals, their potential meeting in Riyadh would renew one of the biggest rivalries in men's tennis.

title: LIV Golf sent warning over Australia event: "We are monitoring it pretty closely"
article_text:
Australian MP Peter Malinauskas has warned LIV Golf the country won't be interested in staging one of the breakaway tour's most popular events should they not secure star names such as Cameron Smith.

LIV Golf's future is far from certain after the league filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States in September.

Sources indicate LIV are extremely confident that it will bounce back in 2027 with some players from its existing roster and some new recruits.

LIV were handed a boost earlier in the week after reportedly receiving commitments from 15 golfers to take part in a re-imagined version of the league, dubbed "2.0".

But several notables have already walked away, indicating that they want no part of LIV's new era.

The latest departures have intensified doubts over whether the league can assemble a strong enough field to justify bringing its popular Adelaide tournament back in 2027.

Former US Open champion Graeme McDowell became the latest high-profile name to reject the proposed relaunch, while Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton, Ian Poulter, Sergio Garcia, Louis Oosthuizen and Tom McKibbin have also announced they are moving on.

Australian Lucas Herbert has confirmed he will leave LIV to pursue a return to the DP World Tour, dealing another significant blow to the all-Australian Ripper GC.

Attention now turns to captain Smith, the 2022 Open champion, whose future remains uncertain.

Court documents reveal he has sought a release from his LIV contract, although he has yet to publicly confirm his plans.

Smith previously indicated he was open to the idea of staying, but wanted more answers from LIV's leadership before making a decision.

Malinauskas, the South Australian premier, has made clear that LIV's assurances alone will not guarantee the tournament's return.

"It's tricky," he told Australian radio station SEN.

"LIV Golf are officially telling us that they are all systems go to be back here.

"But we are monitoring it pretty closely. What's happening with the players is going to be the most instructive outcome here.

"It's very important to us they keep the likes of Cam Smith and Bryson DeChambeau in that playing roster; that underpins the success of the event."

He added: "We're not going to go through with LIV unless they put on the standard of event they have put on in the past, which has been truly exceptional."

LIV is attempting to secure new investment after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund withdrew its financial backing.

London-based private equity firm BC Partners has offered up to $300m to support a revamped 2027 circuit, conditional on sufficient player commitments.

A soft deadline of 25 October was in place, though reports suggest it has been pushed back by five days.

That deadline has been extended to October 30, leaving the league with little time to resolve its roster and financial uncertainty.

Meanwhile, LIV has announced the appointment of former Taylor Made and Adidas executive Mark King as senior adviser.

King, who will begin the role effective immediately, brings a wealth of experience and is one of the most respected executives in the golf industry.

Telegraph Sport reported in October 2022 he was lined up to replace Greg Norman as the commissioner, with the former Open champion "moved upstairs".

King said: "Having spent much of my career in golf, I believe there is a tremendous opportunity for LIV Golf to establish itself as a competitive and enduring force in the game."

In the same announcement, the league said it "remains laser focused on advancing its conversations with players regarding their participation" in LIV 2.0.

The lawyer representing LIV told a bankruptcy court hearing earlier this month it needed to sign a "sufficient number of players to have a bona fide golf league".

The lawyer added LIV would know by the end of October whether it could proceed with LIV 2.0 or move to winding down the breakaway league.

LIV claim they are still generating "inbound interest from established, elite professionals and emerging talent across global professional golf".

title: LIV Adelaide on the brink as major champ joins player exodus
article_text:
As another major champion confirmed he was leaving LIV Golf, the South Australian premier made it clear only a star-studded line-up would keep the Adelaide event alive in 2027, with its fate to be decided sooner rather than later.

- A wave of player exits, including Graeme McDowell, Jon Rahm and Sergio Garcia, threatens LIV's ability to deliver the Adelaide event to the standard required by its contract.

- South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas says LIV has told officials it's "all systems go" for 2027, but warns the government won't proceed unless the standard of event is met.

- The player commitment deadline tied to BC Partners' $300m funding pledge has been extended to October 30 amid ongoing US bankruptcy hearings.

A commitment from Cameron Smith to LIV 2.0 may not be enough to keep the event in Adelaide, with a flurry of exits unlikely to allow officials to deliver the “standard of event” the contract with the South Australian government demands.

Former US Open champion Graeme McDowell has become the latest addition to a list which already includes headline acts Jon Rahm, Sergio Garcia and Australian Lucas Herbert as players who won’t be a part of LIV in 2027.

A deadline for player commitments, needed for BC Partners to follow through with a pledge of $300m in funding for the embattled league, has been extended to October 30 as bankruptcy hearings continue in the US.

However, before the deadline, Rahm and his Legion XIII team-mates Tyrell Hatton and Tom McKibbin, have confirmed their exits, while the fourth member, Caleb Surratt, played in the Hong Kong Open with no LIV logos on his clothing.

Sergio Garcia, David Puig, Louis Oosthuizen, Brandon Grace, Ian Poulter, Abraham Ancer, Thomas Pieters and Adrian Meronk are among those who have declared their intentions to play elsewhere in 2027 and beyond.

Smith, the 2022 Open Champion, is yet to confirm his plans, but it has been reported the Australian is among a host of players, including Ripper GC team-mate Marc Leishman, to have formally requested a release from his LIV Golf contract at the ongoing bankruptcy hearings.

South Australian Premier, Peter Malinauskas said his government had indications from LIV officials that it was “all systems go” for the 2027 Adelaide event, to be staged at Kooyonga Golf Club.

However, if Smith joins the list of departures, the lack of star power (with only Bryson DeChambeau and Dustin Johnson arguably remaining as players of significant calibre) could prove the death knell.

“It’s tricky. LIV Golf are officially telling us that they are all systems go to be back here,” Malinauskas told radio station SEN this week.

“But we are monitoring it pretty closely. What’s happening with the players is going to be the most instructive outcome here.

“It’s very important to us they keep the likes of Cam Smith and Bryson DeChambeau in that playing roster; that underpins the success of the event. That’s something we are monitoring closely just to see how it unfolds.

“We’re not going to go through with LIV unless they put on the standard of event they have put on in the past, which has been truly exceptional.

“We’re going to know for sure in the next two to three weeks.”

Amid various reports around LIV 2.0, it's been suggested officials have commitments from up to 15 players to be a part of what would be a scaled-back, 10-tournament series of events around the world with significantly reduced prizemoney.

It has also been reported Johnson is part of a group of more than 10 players, including Bubba Watson and Thomas Detry, who are set to take on the Saudi Public Investment Fund, LIV’s original backers who ploughed more than $6 billion into the league before pulling funding for more than $100 million in "severance payments".

As part of that action, they have refused to sign a new agreement until those claims are actioned, adding to the concern over LIV’s future in Adelaide.

title: PGA Tour star agreed secret LIV Golf deal before career-defining U-turn
article_text:
Life is full of sliding doors moments. A few of those, in the money-crazed bubble of golf at least, came in the summer of 2022 shortly after the civil war that would rip the sport apart ignited.

A number of stars, some rising and others fading, had to decide whether to accept unimaginable riches and join the controversial Saudi-backed LIV Golf Invitational, as it was known then, or relent and remain with the PGA Tour. Four years on, those decisions have had lasting impacts upon careers and – to a lesser extent – legacies.

However, it is impossible to predict just how consequential a move to LIV would have been to the career trajectory of one of the very best players in the world.

At the time, LIV’s interest in Cam Young was well known.

His breakthrough year in 2022 had included top five finishes at both the PGA Championship and The Open. A PGA Tour win was surely around the corner.

But Young was seriously interested in ditching the PGA Tour for LIV, and it has been revealed in recent bankruptcy filings just how close the American was to crossing the divide.

The filings show that four years ago, Young signed an “intent-to-play” agreement with LIV which would have made him one of the biggest coups for then CEO Greg Norman before LIV’s second season.

“Frankly, I have decided to stay,” Young eventually confirmed at the 2022 Tour Championship. “So, I don’t know, it’s a really difficult situation because it’s not really anything anyone wanted to happen.

“I think it wasn’t meant to be this hostile between the two. Frankly, throughout the whole process with [LIV], I was very interested. I think they have a bunch of good ideas and are doing some cool stuff.

“With some of the changes coming [to the PGA Tour], that’s kind of what really helped me decide to kind of stay and pursue those goals that I have for myself, like making a Presidents Cup team and a Ryder Cup team and winning a major when all of that is just uncertain if you go. It’s a tough place for me because, you know, I’m very young and there are a lot of factors.”

Young does not have a major in his locker yet and his career did not in kickstart in 2023. In fact, his struggle to win a PGA Tour title remained a desperate storyline for another couple of seasons.

But Young is now a bona fide star. He is ranked fourth in the world, the current Players champion, and he has played pivotal roles on Presidents Cup and Ryder Cup teams, just like he had dreamed.

LIV has proved less fertile ground for emerging stars in recent years, owing to the league’s struggle to secure world ranking points and therefore clear pathways into the majors. When Young signed his initial agreement – dated July 24, 2022, exactly a week after his runner-up finish in the Open at St Andrews – he knew he was preparing to take a big leap of faith.

And perhaps Young was always destined to reside among the very elite regardless.

But he will also feel vindicated that he trusted his instincts with a change of heart that has indisputably altered the course of his career.

title: LIV Golf’s future and its ripple effect on the PGA Tour and DP World Tour
article_text:
LIV Golf didn’t generate this much suspense at tournaments when the music was blaring, the Saudi cash was flowing freely and players from the Cleeks and Majestics headed off in carts for the shotgun start.

Every day, there’s more speculation. Who’s leaving? Who’s staying? Weren’t these the same questions four years ago?

It was May 31, 2022, when a group of golf writers out to dinner in Ohio received emails announcing the field for the inaugural LIV Golf event — Dustin Johnson and 12 other PGA Tour members — and had to leave before the Crème brûlée arrived.

And now another waiting game, not for the launch but whether LIV survives.

LIV Golf is working through Chapter 11 bankruptcy with a pledge of $300 million from BC Partners Credit, a far cry from the $5 billion the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia dropped in four years before abruptly pulling the plug.

Key to the “LIV 2.0” version — at least 10 tournaments, player equity and prize money half of what it used to be — is getting a “critical mass” of players to buy into the plan. How many players comprise a critical mass is unclear. And while LIV officials don’t plan to announce each decision piecemeal, players are doing that for them.

Jon Rahm and Sergio Garcia have court-approved separations from LIV and are free to go. Louis Oosthuizen, Ian Poulter, Tom McKibbin and Adrian Meronk have said they are leaving. Graeme McDowell added his name to the list Monday with a succinct message on social media.

Adding a wrinkle to the immediate future of LIV was a report by The Athletic that Johnson was among more than 10 players seeking severance deals from PIF worth more than $100 million in contract payments. Johnson’s attorney suggested a deal was tied to players sticking with LIV 2.0.

“The decision to release potential claims against the PIF and join LIV 2.0 will be influenced largely by how the PIF manages the windup of LIV 1.0,” David Cornwell told The Athletic.

An amended restructuring agreement approved by the New Jersey bankruptcy court indicates LIV no longer has a hard deadline for players to decide. The hope was to have a decision by the end of the month. LIV remains bullish about a 2027 season.

That won’t be the end of the drama, however, and it would seem the golf landscape is still a long way off from being stitched back together, if it ever can be.

The PGA Tour has yet to say whether defectors — currently banned for one year from the date of their last LIV appearance — have a place. It’s not a high priority as the tour seeks to fill out its lucrative “Championship Series” schedule in 2028 and find sponsors for the second tier.

The DP World tour, meanwhile, delivered a strong ultimatum when CEO Guy Kinnings said anyone staying with LIV need not apply for membership.

That made it an easy choice for Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton — particularly with Ryder Cup strings attached — and for youngsters Tom McKibbin and David Puig. They have status based on performance. That doesn’t mean it sits well with those who stayed.

“Four years ago, they didn’t give a (crap) about the DP World Tour,” Joost Luiten told Today’s Golfer. “They made a decision to go after the money. And now all of a sudden, the money is gone and they want to come back and act like nothing happened. I don’t think that’s right.”

There’s also the matter of sponsor exemptions for those who don’t have status, or even those who never gave much thought to the DP World Tour because they didn’t need it. Now they do.

DP World Tour officials are not in position to turn their back on a chance to strengthen fields.

“Given the high volume of inbound interest and enquiries we have received in recent weeks, we are exploring the terms on which we are willing to accommodate players provided they are free from third party contractual restrictions and are willing to abide by our membership regulations,” a DP World Tour spokesman said.

It’s possible such players are allowed only a set number of exemptions. And because the exemptions are for stock events — think Magical Kenya Open and the Soudal Open in Belgium — it might not be a case of squeezing out a more worthy player.

But then it’s a matter of whether loyalty means more than name recognition.

Eddie Pepperell, among the most thoughtful players, missed the cut last week in South Korea and wound up one spot out of a full DP World Tour card for 2027. He wrote in his “The Chipping Forecast” post that outside of players whom people pay to watch, send everyone else to Q-school.

But potentially losing a spot in the field to a player no longer interested in LIV because it no longer offers $20 million purses with no cuts?

“As someone who has gone through the wringer this game provides (mostly due to my own shortcomings of course) in recent years, and who has gone back to Q School and had two immensely divergent experiences, betrayal feels like the right word,” Pepperell wrote. “And unfortunately, when one feels that way inevitably what follows is a loss of respect, and what tends to fill the void left behind is resentment and contempt.”

title: Genoa breaks free from A-Cap as club CEO shows optimism about new era
article_text:
Genoa CFC is optimistic about a new era under majority owner Dan Șucu after finally breaking free from an agitated relationship with A-Cap. A recent legal victory for the Serie A club brought greater clarity to its ownership, opening the door to new financial partnerships and a more football-focused strategy.

On 23 June, a Genoa court rejected A-Cap’s challenge to the club’s recapitalisation for the third time, following 18 months of litigation. A-Cap retains a minority stake of around 22 per cent, but CEO Andrés Blázquez has guaranteed it has “zero involvement” in the club’s governance.

“It confirmed that the right decision had been made for Genoa’s benefit and validated what we had known all along. We moved on from a difficult relationship with a former owner who is now facing several widely publicized investigations in the United States”, Blazquez said.

The dispute has cost the club millions of euros in legal fees, according to the CEO, while also creating challenges in dealings with financial institutions and other stakeholders. With Dan Șucu established as majority owner since December 2024, Genoa now wants to improve its financial position and attract new partners without the uncertainty surrounding its previous ownership structure.

“From the moment Mr Șucu came on board, the legal implications were never in question, as he had a clear vision for Genoa and a well-defined purpose behind his investment”, affirmed Blazquez.

Șucu has been committed to the club from the outset, arriving when the business was close to bankruptcy. The priority now is to continue strengthening the balance sheet, improve the club’s financial health and maintain investment in the squad.

A-Cap’s involvement came at a sporting cost as well. Genoa missed opportunities to sign Djed Spence for €7 million and goalkeeper David de Gea on a free transfer after the proposals were rejected under the previous ownership.

“A-Cap said: ‘He is an old-style goalkeeper; we shouldn’t get him,” revealed Blazquez.

The CEO has also stated that Mason Greenwood had been offered to the club at a time when his valuation still had potential to rise exponentially. He estimates that Genoa may have lost €70 million to €80 million in player value because people without a football-focused approach influenced sporting decisions.

“We weren’t able to make decisions based on sporting considerations. Those situations would have been different if Mr Șucu had been in control at the time.” Blazquez says.

For Genoa, the end of A-Cap’s influence is not simply the conclusion of a lengthy legal dispute. It is an opportunity to rebuild relationships with financial partners and align sporting decisions with the club’s wider business strategy.

title: NBA partners with Polymarket, Kalshi for predictions market oversight
article_text:
In a controversial move, US basketball’s elite NBA has struck a pair of new partnerships with prominent prediction market operators Polymarket and Kalshi, becoming the latest major US sports property to wade into the ongoing trend.

Going forward, both operators will now be able to leverage NBA data, statistics, and, perhaps crucially, NBA intellectual property (including logos and imagery) in their operations as the league’s ‘preferred prediction-market exchanges’.

Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms.

In return, the league will be able to govern what NBA-related markets the pair can and cannot offer, as well as prohibit trading on NBA events by all league and team personnel, with the NBA also to collaborate with Polymarket and Kalshi for information sharing around any investigations regarding illicit and suspicious trading.

To facilitate the agreement, the NBA has struck a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the United States Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), the regulatory body that oversees the prediction market industry) to ensure proper oversight of the prediction market business.

On that element, NBA head of media distribution and partnerships Scott Kaufman-Ross said: “As this category develops, we believe it is important to work constructively with regulators and operators to help ensure that appropriate safeguards are in place. These partnerships represent an important step in establishing a framework that creates new opportunities to engage our fans.”

In this regard, the NBA is following the lead of the National Hockey League, Major League Soccer, UFC, and Major League Baseball, all of which struck agreements with Polymarket and/or Kalshi in the past year.

The NBA is, perhaps, the most prominent among all of these sports properties, and second in the US only to the NFL in terms of reach.

The NFL remains the last major men’s sports property in the US without a Polymarket or Kalshi partnership, and that may remain the case for the foreseeable future, according to comments NFL commissioner Roger Goodell made last month.

In a September interview, Goodell said that the NFL would not partner with either until there are stronger federal guardrails, stating: “We think that there needs to be stronger regulations in the prediction markets.

"We want to see that to protect the integrity of our game. We want to make sure we're protecting the consumers that are on those platforms for the NFL."

The NFL is not wanting for sponsorship revenue, and clearly would much rather wait to see how ongoing regulatory disputes involving Polymarket and Kalshi play out, while the NBA has taken the opposite approach, seeking to enter the space early in order to prevent malpractice in the interim and in effect take control of its destiny.

Weightlifting becomes first sport to take global event back to Russia
article_text:
Weightlifting is set to become the first Olympic sport to take a global championships back into Russia, since that country invaded Ukraine in 2022.

Over the weekend, the International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) unveiled that the 2030 Weightlifting Championships will take place in Russia's capital city of Moscow (while also announcing the hosts of three other world championships).

Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms.

Indeed, this comes only four months after the IWF made Russian athletes eligible once again to compete in its events – they had also been banned by the sport's authorities since early 2022.

For the last 4.5 years, no world championships in any Olympic sport have taken place in Russia.

Jose Quinones, general secretary at the IWF, commented: "All the bids we received were excellent and we are sure that the championships in your respective countries will be a huge success."

The event will also be a qualifying tournament for weightlifting at the 2032 Summer Olympic Games in Brisbane, Australia.

The Russian Weightlifting Federation, meanwhile, stated that it is "the first Olympic sports federation to succeed in bringing a top-level official competition back to the country in many years."

All this from the IWF follows on from the International Olympic Committee (IOC) provisionally lifting its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee, in July. Russian athletes have actually been banned from competing at the Olympics under their own flag since 2016, because of state-sponsored doping offences prior to the invasion of Ukraine.

The ROC was invited back in from the cold after accepting that it no longer controlled sporting bodies in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.

However, the IOC’s decision does come with some caveats. All Russian athletes returning to international competition must meet relevant anti-doping requirements, while the IOC will not organise events in Russia or invite Russian government or state officials to its events.

The Olympic body will also decide on the display of the Russian flag, anthem, colours, or any identifications for the Olympic Games “at the appropriate time.”

Following the IOC's decision, an appeal against it was immediately filed by Ukraine.

Only 27 athletes from Russia competed across the 2024 Olympics in Paris and the 2026 Winter Games in Milano Cortina – as neutrals – after undergoing a vetting process to ensure they did not publicly support the war in Ukraine.

This has now been scrapped, with Russian athletes only having to abide by the values of the Olympic charter.

The IOC has, however, left it up to individual sports federations to decide on whether Russia should be allowed to host major events again; out of these, the IWF has been the first to stick its head above the parapet on the issue.

title: Jannik Sinner makes telling injury comment as he is asked if tennis is ‘breaking his body’
article_text:
Jannik Sinner has highlighted the importance of having “a long-term vision” in tennis as he addressed whether the sport is too physically demanding.

The Italian star has been sidelined due to a right knee injury since he defeated Alexander Zverev in the Wimbledon final in July to defend his title at the All England Club.

Having already missed the North American summer hard-court season and withdrawn from the Asian swing, Sinner confirmed on 6 October that his 2026 season was over.

“Hello everyone, I would like to give you a little update,” the five-time Grand Slam champion said in a video on social media.

“Me, together with the doctors, have decided that I need a course of treatment for my knee, which means that the 2026 season is officially over.

“The last couple of years, especially the ending in Turin, gave me so many beautiful feelings and emotions, which this year is going to be way different, but at the moment I also need to think about my long-term career, so I will do everything possible to get back a hundred percent.

“I will thank you already in advance for your support and hope to see you very, very soon on court again. Ciao ciao!”

Want more from Tennis365? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for tennis coverage you can trust.

While Sinner has not shared details about the specific nature of his knee injury, Sky Sport Italy have reported that the issue he is dealing with is iliotibial band syndrome (ITBS).

Sinner is not the only high-profile ATP star to suffer a significant injury in 2026, with Carlos Alcaraz, Jack Draper and Lorenzo Musetti also having been sidelined.

In an interview with Italian newspaper la Repubblica, Sinner was asked if tennis was “breaking” his body.

Q. But isn’t it just that this tennis is breaking your body too much? An ankle buckles, a kneecap dislocates, a wrist can no longer handle thousands of accelerations, a hip wears out from twisting. Nowadays, there’s no tournament without withdrawals.

Sinner: Injuries are part of sport. You have to be smart and understand how much and when to play.

You need to have a long-term vision. Today isn’t the only thing to consider; you sow now, but the harvest comes later.

And the difference is always made by hard work and preparation, not luck. That helps you win a point, not the match itself.

title: Novak Djokovic issues major updates on his 2027 schedule and ongoing health issues
article_text:
Novak Djokovic has issued an update on his schedule as he looked ahead to 2027, while he has also made a telling comment about the health problems that have troubled him this season.

The 24-time Grand Slam champion spoke about his struggles with physical issues after losing his opening matches at the Cincinnati Masters and the US Open.

After collapsing to a shock five-set defeat to Mariano Navone at the US Open, Djokovic said: “I think it was obvious that it was an awful feeling for me on the court.

“It’s something that I’ve been carrying, unfortunately, pretty much every match this year: vomiting, throwing up, a serious issue there.

“Then my whole body starts to collapse, cramping and pain. The back just gave up in the end, and shoulder, and I couldn’t close it out.”

Djokovic discussed the health concerns again after his battling second round win against Bu Yunchaokete at the China Open earlier this month, and he suggested he had made a breakthrough.

“I don’t want to be revealing what it is, but I’m trying to get to the bottom of it with my team. Sometimes it works better, sometimes it doesn’t,” explained the Serb.

Want more from Tennis365? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for tennis coverage you can trust.

“Today, again, for first couple sets… Actually, surprisingly something I haven’t experienced this year so far, that in the third set I kind of broke through.

“I felt better. Towards the end of the second and all third set, I felt fresher than I have in the beginning of the match.”

Djokovic went on to secure his 102nd career singles title at the ATP 500 tournament in Beijing.

In an interview with Serbian website Sportal, Djokovic divulged he is “close” to finding a solution to the problem.

“It’s progressed a lot and we’re on the right track, it’s not 100% yet, but I’m close,” the 39-year-old said (translated from Serbian).

The former world No 1 went on to confirm he will play the rescheduled Six Kings Slam exhibition in December while also revealing he will compete at the 2027 Australian Open.

“I will be playing at the Six Kings exhibition in Saudi Arabia,” Djokovic said.

“For the next season, I know for sure that I will be in Australia. I will see if I will play a tournament before the Australian Open or not. I will decide in agreement with the team.

“Now, the concentration is to finish the season as well as possible.”

Djokovic, who will play at the Swiss Indoors in Basel this week, added: “I didn’t play Basel for a long time.

“The schedule changed, they moved the tournament in Saudi Arabia that I was supposed to play, so that week was free.

“I’m playing well, I’m feeling good. Of course, it’s not the way we want it yet, but at a competitive level.”

title: HYLO Open: one last European stop
article_text:
The European leg of the HSBC BWF World Tour reaches its final stop in Saarbrücken this week. With some big names resting, the HYLO Open 2026 gives Europe’s top players one last chance to build on a strong autumn.

Play at the Saarlandhalle begins this morning with qualification. William Bøgebjerg, Miranda Wilson and Jan Colin Völker/Emma Moszczynski are among those chasing a place in the main draw, which opens this afternoon with the first round of men’s doubles and women’s doubles.

Indonesia’s Sabar Karyaman Gutama/Moh Reza Pahlevi Isfahani top the men’s doubles draw, and Chinese Taipei’s Hsu Yin-Hui/Lin Jhih Yun lead the women’s doubles. Europe has plenty of contenders. In men’s doubles, England’s Ben Lane/Sean Vendy and Denmark’s Daniel Lundgaard/Mads Vestergaard are two of the pairs to watch. In women’s doubles, Bulgaria’s Gabriela Stoeva/Stefani Stoeva are in the mix as well as France’s Margot Lambert/Camille Pognante who are the defending Champions of the HYLO Open.

The remaining disciplines start tomorrow, and the men’s singles draw has a familiar name at the top. Anders Antonsen is the top seed after a busy European run: he won the Arctic Open and finished runner-up on home soil at the Denmark Open, before a first-round exit in Paris last week. Saarbrücken gives the Dane a chance to finish the swing with a third podium.

He will not have it easy. Third seed Alex Lanier, the reigning world champion who defeated Antonsen in the Odense final, is also in the draw, along with sixth seed Toma Junior Popov.

The women’s singles field is also competitive. Line Christophersen is seeded third, and Line Højmark Kjærsfeldt is also among the seeds. Strong opposition comes from outside the continent, led by second seed Pusarla V. Sindhu, who arrives after finishing runner-up at the French Open.

Mixed doubles has one of the strongest European line-ups of the week. Thom Gicquel/Delphine Delrue, the reigning world champions, are the second seeds. Germany’s Marvin Seidel/Thuc Phuong Nguyen are seeded eighth and will hope for home support in Saarbrücken.

Several big names have withdrawn after a busy stretch of tournaments. Christo Popov is out after winning the French Open on Sunday, a title that lifts him to world number one. Mia Blichfeldt, champion here in both 2024 and 2025, has also withdrawn. So have Mathias Christiansen/Alexandra Bøje, last year’s mixed doubles winners.

title: DP World Tour chiefs accused of "betraying" members with "galling" LIV Golf stance
article_text:
England's Eddie Pepperell says he fears feeling resentful towards the DP World Tour over its stance on allowing a select number of LIV Golf players to tee it up on the circuit in 2027.

The European Tour confirmed at the beginning of the month that those signing up to LIV's proposed new era will be prohibited from holding membership next season.

Its hard-line stance, which is at odds with how it has previously dealt with LIV players, appeared to send multiple golfers towards the exit door as it scrambles to emerge from the ashes without Saudi Arabia's backing.

But the approach has ruffled feathers among some members, with Dutch veteran Joost Luiten the most outspoken on the topic.

Luiten told GolfMagic he viewed it as a 'weak' decision to allow LIV players back onto the circuit easily.

He said sponsor invites should be reserved for young talents embarking on their careers or those who 'stayed loyal'.

Pepperell, who was among those to lose their cards at the Genesis Championship, wrote a lengthy column on Substack over the weekend after DP World Tour members Ewen Ferguson, Richard Mansell and Marco Penge offered their two cents.

Ferguson said it was "hilarious" that those who were critical of the DP World Tour now believe it is the "best thing since sliced bread".

Pepperell told the latest edition of the Chipping Forecast: "I saw Ewen Ferguson, Richard Mansell and Joost Luiten about a week ago all comment on this.

"And comment, I would say, quite unfavourably on it in terms of their opinions towards the DP World Tour on the rumours. And they are mostly still rumours that invites really are going to be given to some of these players.

"I think that is confirmed at this point. I don't think it's really speculation to say that Charles Howell III is going to be playing on the DP World Tour next year a number of times through invites.

"And I think it's that galling, frankly."

Pepperell was referring to the fact that the DP World Tour is currently in negotiations with several LIV Golf players who are out of contract but not exempt for next season about playing opportunities.

The discussions are aimed at reaching agreements that would guarantee them invites to a select number of tournaments outside the Rolex Series.

Charles Howell III is among the group, but some have expressed the view that the 47-year-old should not receive favourable treatment, given he has spent the entirety of his career playing almost exclusively in the United States.

"I've not got anything against Charles Howell III," stressed Pepperell.

"And I just want to point out too, it's not that I'm under any impression that these guys are not better at golf than me.

"Lucas Herbert is a better golfer than me. I'm not of the opinion he shouldn't be playing on the DP World Tour immediately because he's not a better player than me.

"My point is quite simple to those that don't get it. And it's a small minority. It's to earn your right the way I did at Q-School. The way we all have to.

"And to the degree to which a player hasn't earned their right historically, a la, say, Rory McIlroy, when he was offered invites in the very early stages of his career, it's a very different scenario.

"Because there's somebody that didn't play on LIV Golf before receiving those invites. And of course LIV Golf has done an awful lot of harm to the DP World Tour.

"So yeah, I do find it quite, as I described in the article, and I tried to be fair within it, but I did see it as a bit of a betrayal from the Tour to be giving invites to such players, frankly."

It has been suggested that the DP World Tour's move to ban LIV players is simply because officials at Wentworth HQ smell blood.

Pepperell said he believes LIV is "already done for", adding: "If it couldn't succeed with $6bn behind it, there is no way it's ever going to succeed with a mere $300m behind it, of which, actually, the more people I listen to talk about this investment, they describe it more as a debt investment on the side of BC Partners to offset their own future tax liabilities more than anything else, frankly.

"I can understand the idea that this will kill LIV off. I think it will. But my view is it was already dead.

"And so you didn't need to bend over to give Charles Howell III or Thomas Pieters [invites].

"And I like Thomas Pieters. I've got an awful lot of time for him. I think he's a brilliant player.

"But I just think he should go back to Q-School the way I did, the way Kiradech [Aphibarnrat] might have to, the way a lot of players have to, and earn your status.

"I'm not of the opinion they won't do so. I think they're plenty good enough to do so. But make them do it.

"You know, it's the meritocratic beauty of a sport like golf. It's a cornerstone that I'm unbending on, frankly, and always have been."

Pepperell said a calculation needs to be made over which players should receive invites.

"I have no issue with Joaquin Niemann coming back and receiving invites," he said. "He's a star. I would watch it. I'd pay to watch Joaquin Niemann play golf. I wouldn't pay to watch Charles Howell III play golf. Nothing against him.

title: LIV Golf Adelaide Chief Sets Ultimatum To The Circuit After Player Exodus
article_text:
The main story currently surrounding LIV Golf involves the players, specifically who is committing to LIV 2.0 and who is wanting out from the circuit.

A deadline of October 25th had been set, but that has been extended to October 30th, with little detail known about what the new schedule for LIV 2.0 will actually look like.

Reports claim it will be a 10-event schedule in 2027, split between five tournaments in the United States and five international events.

One of those international tournaments, given its success, is potentially going to be Australia, but that will depend on one big factor.

LIV Golf Adelaide has been the circuit's jewel in the crown since 2023, with its attendance figures and atmosphere on the ground earning the prize of the World’s Best Golf Event at the World Golf Awards for three consecutive years (2023, 2024, and 2025).

However, with the future of the League uncertain, especially with the mass exodus of players like Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton, it's left the question of will the events go ahead or not?

Speaking on Australian radio station SEN, South Australian Premier, Peter Malinauskas, revealed there had been indications from LIV officials that the event in 2027 will go ahead, but it was being monitored by tournament officials.

"It’s tricky. LIV Golf are officially telling us that they are all systems go to be back here," Malinauskas explained to SEN this week.

"We are monitoring it pretty closely. What’s happening with the players is going to be the most instructive outcome here.

"It’s very important to us they keep the likes of Cam Smith and Bryson DeChambeau in that playing roster; that underpins the success of the event. That’s something we are monitoring closely just to see how it unfolds.

"We’re not going to go through with LIV unless they put on the standard of event they have put on in the past, which has been truly exceptional.

"We’re going to know for sure in the next two to three weeks."

In 2025, the LIV Golf League and the South Australia Government confirmed that Adelaide would be the home of LIV Golf in Australia, with an extension agreement going through until 2031.

However, with just a handful of names committing to LIV Golf 2.0, including Richard Bland, Cameron Tringale and Brendan Steele, the possibility of events taking place up until 2031 appear less likely to what they were 18 months ago.

What's more, further recent reports are claiming that Dustin Johnson is one of many LIV Golfers attempting to negotiate with Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, the original backers of LIV, in an attempt to receive money for their unpaid LIV Golf contracts.

First reported by The Athletic, it's been alleged that the 10 players involved have refused to sign a new agreement with LIV 2.0 until their claims are addressed.

In terms of LIV Golf themselves, the circuit recently confirmed that former TaylorMade executive, Mark King, has been signed to chair its Advisory Board.

Following the appointment, the League claims it remains "on track" to secure the support needed to reach its new era.
